lessons.text: Label every actor with an explicit ID and role (e.g. 'lw', 'rw') and place them at coordinates that match standard top-down attacking orientation (left→right: left wing occupies lower half of rink, right wing upper half) — never let the answer key reference a role that isn't spatially verified against the diagram.

Before finalizing the correct answer, confirm the named player has no defender within ~0.15 normalized units; if the nearest defender is closer than that, the player does not have time and space and must not be the answer.
Always place every actor referenced in the question stem or answer choices on the diagram — if a player is mentioned or selectable, they must be visible.
Assign each defender a clear role relative to a specific actor (pressuring the puck carrier, shadowing a teammate, patrolling a lane) so their positioning creates an unambiguous read.
Assign a unique, meaningful id to every selectable actor before writing the answer key — the correct ids[] entries must exactly match actor id fields in the scene.

Place actors so that exactly one occupies the geometrically distinct zone the question targets (e.g., blind-side, behind the receiver); if multiple actors qualify, the correct pick is arbitrary and the question is broken.
Separate any two actors sharing a role (e.g., puck carrier vs. nearby teammate) by at least 0.12 normalized units on both axes so each actor reads as distinct on the rendered rink.
Cap total actor count at five for U9 scenarios; if the concept requires a contrast, remove redundant actors and preserve the single clearest open-vs-covered pair.
Assign every actor a unique, explicit ID that matches the IDs referenced in answers and scoring logic — never rely on kind alone to identify a target.
If the question stem implies movement, include motion cues (facing, path, or vector) on every relevant actor; never pair 'moving' or 'developing' language with a static-positions-only snapshot.

Place each defender on or within ~0.05 units of the direct puck-to-net line at a realistic closing distance (1–3 strides) — never float a defender off that line into open space unless their role is explicitly intercepting a pass lane, not the puck-carrier.

Ensure every actor has meaningful separation from its nearest neighbor: no two actors should share both x and y within 0.08 units, and any 'available' passing target must have at least 0.10 units of clear space from the nearest defender to read as genuinely open.
